posts.title: The chestnut weeks
posts.excerpt: For about five weeks each autumn the kitchen smells of steamed chestnut. Here is how a kinton is made.
posts.content:
For about five weeks each autumn the kitchen smells of steamed chestnut. Here is how a kinton is made.

Steamed, sieved, gathered

The new-crop chestnuts arrive in sacks from a farm in the hills. We steam them whole, halve them and scoop out the flesh with a small spoon.

Sieved twice and sweetened only a little, the paste is gathered in a damp cotton cloth and twisted once, so each kinton keeps the mark of the hand.

When they run out

When the farm has no more chestnuts, the October tray ends, even if the calendar says there are days left.

A kinton should taste of the chestnut, not of sugar.

Chiyo Amane

posts.title: Azuki at six in the morning
posts.excerpt: Every sweet in the shop begins with a pan of azuki, put on the stove before it is light.
posts.content:
Every sweet in the shop begins with a pan of azuki, put on the stove before it is light.

Four hours, never rushed

The beans soak overnight and cook slowly in the copper pan. The first water is poured away to keep the taste clean.

Sugar goes in last, in three parts, while the paste is stirred with a long wooden paddle.

Smooth or coarse

Koshian is pressed through a fine sieve; tsubuan keeps the skins. Each sweet asks for one or the other.

The beans tell you when they are ready.

Chiyo Amane

posts.title: What to pour beside a wagashi
posts.excerpt: A sweet and a cup of tea are one thing in two parts. A short guide for the table at home.
posts.content:
A sweet and a cup of tea are one thing in two parts. A short guide for the table at home.

Sweet first, then tea

Eat the sweet first and let the tea follow: its bitterness clears the palate and lifts the bean.

Fresh nerikiri like a light sencha; dense yokan likes a stronger cup.

Water a little cool

Seventy degrees for sencha, one minute in the pot. Boiling water makes it harsh.

Tea is the frame; the sweet is the picture.

Shige Amane

posts.title: A moon for September
posts.excerpt: On the night of the harvest moon we stack fifteen white dumplings on a small stand, as our grandparents did.
posts.content:
On the night of the harvest moon we stack fifteen white dumplings on a small stand, as our grandparents did.

Fifteen, in a pyramid

Nine on the bottom, four in the middle, two on top: one for each night of the waxing moon.

The dumplings are plain rice flour and water, rolled smooth by hand.

After the moon

The next day they are grilled lightly and eaten with sweet soy, or simply with tea.

Plain things suit the full moon.

Chiyo Amane

posts.title: The cool of mizu yokan
posts.excerpt: In the hottest weeks we make a softer, wetter yokan that is set with well water and served cold.
posts.content:
In the hottest weeks we make a softer, wetter yokan that is set with well water and served cold.

More water, less sugar

Mizu yokan uses half the sugar of a dense yokan and twice the water, held together by a little kanten.

It should tremble when you set it down.

Serving it

Chill for an hour, cut into thick slices with a damp knife and serve on a glass plate.

Summer sweets should feel like shade.

Shige Amane

posts.title: Wrapping a box in washi
posts.excerpt: Every box leaves the counter wrapped in washi and tied with a cotton cord. Why we still wrap by hand.
posts.content:
Every box leaves the counter wrapped in washi and tied with a cotton cord. Why we still wrap by hand.

The fold

The paper is folded once from the left and once from the right, overlapping as a kimono does, never the other way.

A small slip with the month’s name goes under the cord.

For the person opening it

A box is opened slowly. The wrapping is the first part of the sweet.

A gift should take a little time to open.

Chiyo Amane
